questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: Elizabeth’s religious settlement (1559)
questions.question_text: Outline two key features of Elizabeth I’s 1559 Religious Settlement.
indicative_content: The Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth "Supreme Governor" of the Church of England, requiring all clergy and royal officials to swear an oath of allegiance to her.

The Act of Uniformity established a moderate Protestant Church with the Book of Common Prayer, but kept certain Catholic traditions (priests wearing vestments and churches retaining decorations) to appease moderate Catholics.
questions.examiner_tips: State two distinct features: Supreme Governor title and the Book of Common Prayer/middle way compromises.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Exploration and voyages of discovery
questions.question_text: Analyse the reasons why English overseas voyages and exploration expanded between 1558 and 1588.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: astrolabes, quadrants, and improved navigation
• Optional focus: commercial demand for spices and New World wealth
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Navigational aids: Astrolabes, magnetic compasses, and Mercator projection maps made ocean navigation much safer and more accurate.
Luxury goods: The collapse of the traditional Antwerp cloth market forced English merchants to seek new markets and luxury commodities (spices, silk, tobacco, sugar).
Own knowledge: Ship design (galleons with larger sails and heavier cannons) and rivalry with Spain (privateering and raiding Spanish silver fleets led by Drake and Hawkins).
questions.examiner_tips: Structure 3 distinct PEEL paragraphs covering technology, economic necessity, and Spanish geopolitical rivalry.

questions.topic: Victory Over the Spanish Armada: Naval Tactics vs Weather
questions.spec_topic: KT2.3: The Spanish Armada: reasons for defeat
questions.question_text: ‘Superior English naval tactics were the decisive reason why the Spanish Armada failed in 1588.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: English fireships off Calais
• Optional focus: design and gunnery of Spanish vs race-built galleons
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Naval tactics: Use of 8 fireships at Gravelines broke the Spanish crescent formation; smaller, more manoeuvrable English ships armed with long-range culverin cannons that could reload quickly battered the Spanish.
Spanish weaknesses: Medina Sidonia had no naval experience; supplies rotted in unseasoned wood barrels; Duke of Parma’s army was blockaded in Dutch ports and could not embark.
Weather: The "Protestant Wind" blew the Armada north into treacherous Scottish and Irish waters, wrecking dozens of ships.
Judgement: Fireships forced the Armada into disarray, but severe Atlantic storms caused the actual destruction of the fleet.
questions.examiner_tips: Weigh English tactics against Spanish tactical errors and the decisive role of Atlantic gales.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: Poverty and Elizabethan poor relief
questions.question_text: ‘Tudor attitudes towards poverty and vagrancy remained largely unchanged between 1558 and 1588.’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Houses of Correction (1576 Poor Relief Act)
• Optional focus: harsh punishments mixed with poor rates in the 1572 Vagabonds Act
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing (continuity): Persistent fear of vagabonds and sturdy beggars; harsh physical punishments continued (whipping, boring holes through ears, execution for repeat vagrants under 1572 Act).

Arguments disagreeing (progressive change): Growing recognition of the "deserving poor" (impotent poor: elderly, sick, orphans); 1576 Act to Set the Poor on Work introduced raw materials for work; creation of Houses of Correction (Bridewells) aiming at reform.

Judgement: While punishments remained brutal, the conceptual shift acknowledging that unemployment was caused by economic forces (enclosure, bad harvests) rather than laziness was a major breakthrough.
questions.examiner_tips: Distinguish between the treatment of the "impotent/deserving poor" versus the "idle/sturdy vagabonds".

questions.topic: The Theatre in Early Elizabethan England
questions.spec_topic: KT3.1: Education and leisure: the theatre
questions.question_text: Outline two key features of public theatregoing in Elizabethan England (1558–88).
indicative_content: Purpose-built open-air playhouses were constructed outside the City of London walls (such as The Theatre in 1576 and The Curtain) to avoid City authority bans and Puritan opposition.
Audiences were socially mixed: the poorest spectators (groundlings) paid 1 penny to stand in the open pit around the stage, while wealthier patrons sat in covered tiered galleries.
questions.examiner_tips: Mention purpose-built theatres outside the city walls and the social division between pit groundlings and gallery seats.

questions.topic: Failure of Raleigh’s First Colony in Virginia
questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Attempted colonisation of Virginia: Roanoke
questions.question_text: Analyse why the 1585–86 Roanoke expedition to establish a Virginia colony collapsed.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: deteriorating relations with Wingina and the Secotan Algonquians
• Optional focus: seawater spoiling supplies aboard the flagship Tiger
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Damage to The Tiger: The flagship hit a sandbank on arrival, ruining food supplies and seeds, leaving colonists dependent on Native Americans.
Conflict with Algonquians: Sir Richard Grenville burned an entire village over a stolen silver cup, alienating Chief Wingina and sparking armed attacks.
Own knowledge: Poor selection of colonists: Too many noble "gentlemen" who refused manual labor, and soldiers lacking farming or survival skills.
questions.examiner_tips: Explain the compounding interaction: loss of food stores -> friction with natives -> lack of farming skills among gentlemen.

questions.topic: Catholic Opposition to Elizabeth: Papacy vs Other Factors
questions.spec_topic: KT1.3 & KT2.1: The Catholic challenge: Papacy, Mary Queen of Scots, plots
questions.question_text: ‘Papal hostility was the primary catalyst behind growing Catholic opposition to Elizabeth I between 1559 and 1588.’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Pope Pius V’s 1570 Bull Regnans in Excelsis
• Optional focus: Mary, Queen of Scots’ arrival in England (1568)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Role of Papacy: Pope Pius V issued the Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570), excommunicating Elizabeth and ordering English Catholics to depose her, making loyalty to queen and faith incompatible; missionary priests (Jesuits like Campion) sent to convert.

Role of Mary, Queen of Scots: Mary was a living Catholic figurehead with a legitimate royal claim, inspiring the Northern Earls (1569), Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583), and Babington (1586) plots.
Role of foreign powers: King Philip II of Spain providing financial and military backing to rebels.
Judgement: The Papal Bull provided religious justification, but Mary’s presence in England was the practical catalyst for all plots.
questions.examiner_tips: Address both the theological trigger (1570 Bull) and the practical catalyst (Mary Queen of Scots in England).

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2 & KT3.3: Drake, privateering, circumnavigation, raid on Cadiz
questions.question_text: ‘Sir Francis Drake’s 1587 attack on Cadiz was his greatest contribution to Elizabethan England (1558–88).’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: delaying Armada preparations at Cadiz (1587)
• Optional focus: circumnavigating the globe aboard the Golden Hind (1577–80)
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Raid on Cadiz (1587): Destroyed 30+ Spanish ships and huge stores of seasoned barrel staves, delaying the Armada by over a year and giving England vital time to prepare.

Circumnavigation (1577-80): First Englishman to sail around the globe; claimed New Albion in California; returned with £400,000 of Spanish treasure on the Golden Hind, paying off England’s national debt.
Role in Armada (1588): Vice-Admiral commanding English fleet; captured Spanish flagship Rosario.
Judgement: The raid on Cadiz was militarily crucial, but the circumnavigation brought unmatched global prestige, wealth, and established England as a maritime power.
questions.examiner_tips: Compare the short-term military delay (Cadiz) against long-term national wealth and global prestige (circumnavigation).

questions.topic: Role of Church of England in Society
questions.spec_topic: KT1.2: The Church of England: its role in society
questions.question_text: Outline two key features of how the parish Church of England shaped daily community life after 1559.
indicative_content: The Church acted as a primary source of news and government propaganda, reading royal proclamations and Elizabeth’s approved sermons to parishioners every Sunday.
The Church enforced moral behavior and social order through church courts, punishing drunkenness, adultery, slander, and non-attendance at church services.
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on communication of royal proclamations and moral regulation via church courts.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.3: The nature and extent of the Puritan challenge
questions.question_text: Analyse why Puritan clergy and MPs mounted challenges against the 1559 Religious Settlement.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: controversy over clerical vestments (surplices)
• Optional focus: ornaments and prayer-book rules under the Act of Uniformity
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Vestments controversy: Puritans believed clergy wearing ornate robes (surplices) was unscriptural and too close to Catholic "popish" superstition; Thomas Sampson refused to wear them.
Act of Uniformity: Puritans objected to kneeling for communion, organs, crucifixes, and retaining Catholic saint days.
Own knowledge: Puritan opposition to bishops (demanding a presbyterian system run by elders without hierarchy) and prophecyings (prayer meetings).
questions.examiner_tips: Explain theological objections: vestments, crucifixes, and the hierarchy of bishops.

questions.topic: Tension Between Elizabeth & Mary Queen of Scots
questions.spec_topic: KT1.4 & KT2.1: Mary Queen of Scots claim to throne and plots
questions.question_text: ‘Rivalry between Elizabeth I and Mary, Queen of Scots stemmed mainly from Mary’s dynastic claim to the English crown.’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Catholic doubts over Elizabeth’s legitimacy
• Optional focus: Ridolfi, Throckmorton, and Babington conspiracies
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Mary’s claim: As Henry VII’s great-granddaughter, Catholic Europe viewed Mary as the rightful queen because they regarded Henry VIII’s marriage to Anne Boleyn as invalid and Elizabeth as illegitimate.
Catholic plots: Mary’s presence in England from 1568 provided a focal point for treasonous rebellions (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586).
Religious and foreign threats: Mary’s strong French Guise family connections and Spanish backing.
Judgement: The claim was the legal basis, but Mary’s active involvement in conspiracies to assassinate Elizabeth created the acute, fatal tension.
questions.examiner_tips: Balance Mary’s dynastic legitimacy claim against her practical involvement in assassination conspiracies.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.1: Education and leisure: grammar schools, universities, literacy
questions.question_text: ‘Educational opportunities in England changed very little during the first thirty years of Elizabeth’s reign (1558–88).’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: schooling and domestic training for girls
• Optional focus: expansion of humanist grammar schools for boys
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing (continuity): Girls remained largely excluded from formal education, taught domestic needlework and household management at home; university was restricted to wealthy males; school fees meant lower classes stayed illiterate.

Arguments disagreeing (expansion): Growth of grammar schools teaching Latin, Greek, and debate; petty and dame schools teaching basic literacy; Humanist ideals promoting education to improve society; literacy among wealthy merchants rose significantly.
Judgement: Major expansion of schooling for middle-class boys, but almost total continuity of exclusion for working classes and women.
questions.examiner_tips: Break down by gender and social class: show how boys gained grammar schools while girls and peasants saw little change.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: English involvement in the Netherlands (Treaty of Nonsuch)
questions.question_text: Outline two key features of English military intervention in the Dutch Revolt between 1585 and 1588.
indicative_content: Under the Treaty of Nonsuch (1585), Elizabeth agreed to send 7,400 English soldiers led by Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, to assist the Dutch Protestant rebels.
Leicester’s campaign was undermined by poor military leadership, unpaid soldiers, and his acceptance of the title "Governor-General", which infuriated Elizabeth.
questions.examiner_tips: Mention the Treaty of Nonsuch / Robert Dudley’s expeditionary force and Leicester’s political blunders.

questions.topic: Why Treatment of the Poor Changed 1558-88
questions.spec_topic: KT3.2: Poverty: changing attitudes, 1572 and 1576 Poor Laws
questions.question_text: Analyse why Elizabethan authorities altered how they dealt with poverty and vagabondage between 1558 and 1588.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: parliamentary statutes of 1563, 1572, and 1576
• Optional focus: distinguishing the ‘impotent’ poor from ‘able-bodied’ vagabonds
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Fear of social disorder: Rapid population growth and bad harvests created huge numbers of roaming vagabonds, threatening public order.
Distinction between deserving and undeserving poor: The 1572 Vagabonds Act introduced a local poor rate, while the 1576 Act provided wool and raw materials to put the able-bodied to work.
Own knowledge: Collapse of monastery charity following the Reformation forced local authorities and parliament to step in.
questions.examiner_tips: Highlight the collapse of monastic charity, fear of rebellion, and the categorization of poor into deserving vs idle.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: Situation on Elizabeth’s accession: legitimacy, gender, finances, religion
questions.question_text: ‘Doubts surrounding Elizabeth’s legitimacy posed the gravest threat to her throne upon her accession in 1558.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: contemporary prejudice against a female monarch
• Optional focus: £300,000 Marian Crown debt and war with France
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Legitimacy: Henry VIII had declared Anne Boleyn’s marriage invalid, making Elizabeth illegitimate in the eyes of Catholics who favored Mary Queen of Scots.
Gender: 16th-century prejudice viewed women as weak and unfit to govern or lead armies; pressure to marry risked surrendering England to a foreign prince.
Financial weakness: Mary I left £300,000 of crown debt with high inflation and reliance on foreign loans.
Religious divide: Country bitterly divided between Protestants and Catholics following Mary I’s counter-reformation.
Judgement: While legitimacy invited Catholic challenge, the immediate threat of bankruptcy and foreign invasion from France were more urgent.
questions.examiner_tips: Address legitimacy, gender expectations, crushing crown debt, and the volatile religious division.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.1: The Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569-70
questions.question_text: ‘No domestic threat between 1569 and 1586 endangered Elizabeth I more seriously than the 1569 Revolt of the Northern Earls.’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Westmorland, Northumberland, and the Duke of Norfolk marriage plan
• Optional focus: foreign backing in the Ridolfi, Throckmorton, and Babington plots
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Significance of Northern Earls (1569): Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland mobilized 5,000 armed men, took Durham Cathedral, and aimed to marry Mary to Norfolk and restore Catholicism.

Other plots: Ridolfi Plot (1571) involved the Pope, Philip II, and a planned invasion by the Duke of Alba; Throckmorton Plot (1583) planned French Catholic invasion funded by Spain; Babington Plot (1586) led directly to Mary’s execution.
Judgement: Northern Earls was the only armed military rising on English soil, but foreign-backed assassination conspiracies were far more lethal to Elizabeth personally.
questions.examiner_tips: Compare the armed domestic rising of 1569 against foreign-backed assassination conspiracies (Ridolfi, Throckmorton).

questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: Society and government in Elizabethan England
questions.question_text: Outline two key features of how central and local government operated under Elizabeth I.
indicative_content: The Privy Council, led by William Cecil, met almost daily to advise the Queen on domestic policy, foreign affairs, and national security.
Parliament was summoned only when the monarch needed to pass new laws or approve extraordinary taxation (subsidies).
questions.examiner_tips: Focus on the Privy Council advising the Queen and Parliament’s taxation/law-making functions.

questions.topic: Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots (1587)
questions.spec_topic: KT2.1: Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots (1587)
questions.question_text: Analyse the reasons why Elizabeth I finally authorised the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots in February 1587.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: pressure from Walsingham, Burghley, and the Privy Council
• Optional focus: Mary’s dynastic claim and cipher letters in the Babington Plot
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Privy Council pressure: Walsingham and Cecil were determined to eliminate Mary as a permanent Catholic security threat, passing the Bond of Association.
Babington Plot (1586): Walsingham intercepted Mary’s coded letters explicitly approving the assassination of Elizabeth.
Own knowledge: Rising threat of Spanish invasion: Elizabeth’s councillors argued that England could not face Philip II’s armada with a Catholic claimant inside the realm.
questions.examiner_tips: Link intercepted letters in the Babington Plot directly to the impending threat of the Spanish Armada.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: English involvement in the Netherlands: political, religious, economic rivalry
questions.question_text: ‘Strategic rivalry with Philip II’s Spain was the main motive for England’s direct intervention in the Netherlands (1585–88).’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: signing the Treaty of Nonsuch (August 1585)
• Optional focus: assassination of William of Orange and Antwerp’s cloth trade
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Political rivalry: Spain’s army in the Netherlands (Duke of Parma) was positioned directly across the English Channel, posing a constant invasion threat to England.
Religious solidarity: The assassination of Protestant leader William of Orange (1584) left Dutch Protestants facing annihilation, forcing Elizabeth to intervene under Treaty of Nonsuch.
Economic factors: Netherlands was the main market for England’s cloth trade, and Spanish trade bans crippled English merchants.
Judgement: Geopolitical survival was paramount: Elizabeth could not permit Philip II total control of the Channel coast.
questions.examiner_tips: Weigh strategic invasion fears against religious sympathy and English wool trade interests.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Exploration: technology, trade, rivalry with Spain
questions.question_text: ‘Advances in shipbuilding and navigation were the primary driver of Elizabethan overseas exploration (1558–88).’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: faster, more manoeuvrable galleon hulls and triangular lateen sails
• Optional focus: seeking alternative trade markets after Antwerp’s disruption
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Technology: Galleons with lateen sails, astrolabes, cross-staffs, and accurate magnetic compasses allowed sailors to navigate deep oceans.
Economic necessity: Search for new trade routes to Asia (North-West Passage) and bypassing the Spanish monopoly.
Privateering wealth and royal backing: Drake, Hawkins, and Raleigh backed by royal funding to seize Spanish bullion.
Judgement: Technology made long voyages physically possible, but the lure of immense Spanish plunder was the true motivation.
questions.examiner_tips: Distinguish between the *enabler* (navigation technology) and the *motive* (trade profits and privateering plunder).

questions.spec_topic: KT3.1: Education: grammar schools and universities
questions.question_text: Outline two key features of schooling and university education in Elizabethan England (1558–88).
indicative_content: Grammar schools expanded rapidly to educate middle-class and gentry boys, focusing intensely on Latin, Greek, history, and classical literature.
Education was strictly stratified by gender and wealth: boys from ordinary families attended petty schools or worked, while girls received no formal schooling.
questions.examiner_tips: State the curriculum of grammar schools and the strict social/gender exclusion.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.3: Spanish Armada: reasons for defeat
questions.question_text: Analyse the factors that led to the defeat of Philip II’s Spanish Armada in 1588.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: English naval commanders including Howard, Hawkins, and Drake
• Optional focus: breaking Medina Sidonia’s crescent formation with fireships at Calais
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Fireships at Gravelines: English launched 8 blazing fireships into Calais harbor, causing panic and breaking the Spanish crescent formation.
Superior English naval tactics: Smaller, faster galleons with quick-reloading culverin guns outfought the lumbering Spanish ships.
Own knowledge: Spanish logistical failures (rotting food, poor barrels) and devastating Atlantic storms ("Protestant Wind") wrecking ships.
questions.examiner_tips: Cover tactical disruption (fireships), English gunnery superiority, and Atlantic weather conditions.

questions.topic: Challenge to Religious Settlement: Catholics vs Puritans
questions.spec_topic: KT1.3: Challenge to religious settlement: Puritans and Catholics
questions.question_text: ‘English Catholics posed a far greater challenge than Puritans to Elizabeth’s Religious Settlement during its first decade (1558–68).’ To what extent do you agree with this view?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: enforcement of the 1559 Act of Uniformity
• Optional focus: northern Catholic nobility and recusancy
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Catholic challenge: Recusants refused to attend Protestant church services; Catholic nobility in the North secretly protected priests; danger of foreign intervention from Spain or France.
Puritan challenge: Vestments controversy (1566) where 37 London clergy were suspended; crucifix controversy where Puritan bishops threatened to resign.
Judgement: In the first decade (1558-68), the Puritan challenge within the Church hierarchy was more vocal, though Catholic recusancy harbored greater long-term treasonous potential.
questions.examiner_tips: Confine your answer to the stated 1558-68 period (before Mary Queen of Scots arrived and before Northern Earls revolt).

questions.topic: Failure of the First Colony in Virginia: Planning vs Misfortune
questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Attempted colonisation of Virginia: Roanoke
questions.question_text: ‘Flawed preparation in England was the primary reason why the first Virginia settlement at Roanoke failed.’ To what extent do you agree with this judgement?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: late departure and inadequate agricultural food stores
• Optional focus: leadership tensions between Ralph Lane and Sir Richard Grenville
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Poor planning: Wrong mix of settlers (too many soldiers and gentlemen, too few farmers/artisans); leaving too late in the year to plant crops; reliance on fragile supply ships.
External misfortune: Damage to The Tiger running aground and destroying seeds; severe drought in Virginia.
Hostility with Native Americans: Grenville’s heavy-handed aggression and burning of Algonquian villages provoked warfare.
Judgement: External accidents happened, but the fundamental error was planning a colony with gentlemen who could not feed themselves.
questions.examiner_tips: Weigh human planning errors against natural accidents and hostile native relations.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.1: Elizabethan society: the Great Chain of Being
questions.question_text: Outline one key feature of the social hierarchy in Elizabethan towns or countryside.
indicative_content: Society was organized in a strict hierarchy known as the Great Chain of Being, where everyone had a fixed social rank from the monarch and nobility at the top down to tenant farmers and the landless poor.
questions.examiner_tips: State the strict hierarchical structure (Great Chain of Being) and provide supporting detail on social order.

questions.spec_topic: KT3.3: Exploration and voyages of discovery
questions.question_text: Outline one key feature of English overseas voyages of discovery between 1558 and 1588.
indicative_content: English exploration was heavily motivated by privateering, where sailors like Drake were licensed by royal letters of marque to raid Spanish bullion fleets in the New World.
questions.examiner_tips: Mention privateering raiding Spanish silver ships or the search for new trade routes.

questions.spec_topic: KT2.2: Political, religious, and commercial rivalry with Spain
questions.question_text: Analyse why Anglo-Spanish relations deteriorated into open conflict between 1569 and 1588.
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: Spanish encouragement of English Catholic plots
• Optional focus: English privateering and rivalry over New World trade
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Catholic plots: Philip II funded plots to depose Elizabeth (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583) and welcomed Elizabeth’s excommunication.
Commercial trade and privateering: Drake’s raids on Spanish colonies in the Caribbean and circumnavigation plundered millions in silver.
Own knowledge: Direct English intervention in the Netherlands (Treaty of Nonsuch 1585) where English troops fought the Spanish army directly.
questions.examiner_tips: Cover religious plots, commercial privateering, and direct military conflict in the Netherlands.

questions.spec_topic: KT1.2 & KT1.3: Impact and challenges to religious settlement
questions.question_text: ‘Elizabeth I’s 1559 Religious Settlement largely achieved stability across England by 1588.’ To what extent do you agree with this assessment?
questions.stimulus:
• Optional focus: broad acceptance of the Protestant ‘middle way’
• Optional focus: seminary priests, Jesuits, and Catholic assassination plots
• Incorporate additional historical knowledge of your own.
indicative_content: Arguments agreeing (success): Avoided full-scale religious civil war (unlike France); majority of clergy (9,000+ out of 9,400) swore the oath; created an enduring Church of England that lasted.

Arguments disagreeing (failure): Polarized extremists: Puritans constantly agitated in parliament and through prophecyings; Catholics became treasonous conspirators following the 1570 excommunication; required harsh penal laws and executions of priests.
Judgement: Successful in stabilizing the kingdom and establishing Protestantism, but failed to achieve true national unity.
questions.examiner_tips: Define criteria for "successful": avoidance of civil war versus failure to satisfy religious radicals.
